scope_allowed: Relevance of the validation activities to the COU

models.name: Model-HF
models.what_it_computes: High-fidelity 3D explicit finite element analysis of the delivery system, computing time-resolved actuator force during unsheathing and partial release, including detailed contact, large deformation, and frictional stick–slip.

models.name: Model-RO
models.what_it_computes: Reduced-order explicit FE submodel with homogenized device and sheath representation, computing deployment-force envelopes and peak force estimates under prescribed kinematics.

mechanisms.name: Unsheathing friction and stick–slip
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Peaks in handle force during sheath retraction can cause loss of positional control, abrupt release, or tissue injury.

mechanisms.name: Frame recoil constraint during staged release
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Stored elastic energy in the self-expanding frame generates reaction forces transmitted through the handle; excessive force can lead to overshoot and malposition.

deviation.detail: All credibility factor ratings are reported on a 0–5 Credibility Index (CI), with critical factors requiring CI ≥ 4.0 and non-critical factors requiring CI ≥ 3.5.

expected_decision.outcome_source: The assessment therefore concludes the models are not accepted for the stated context of use.
rationale_keywords: multiple critical criteria fell below the required thresholds

requirements: Critical factors required CI ≥ 4.0 and non-critical factors required CI ≥ 3.5 for acceptance in the stated context of use.

For agreement with bench measurements, the target tolerance on peak forces was set at ±10% for the high-fidelity model and ±12% for the reduced-order model in unsheathing, with time-series root-mean-square error (RMSE) targets at or below 0.3 N and 0.45 N respectively.
For the staged release transient, the tolerance was ±12% for the high-fidelity model and ±15% for the reduced-order model.

For solution accuracy, we sought converged results under time-step refinement such that further halving changed peaks by less than 4% (high-fidelity) and less than 6% (reduced-order), with kinetic-to-internal energy ratios below 5% in Model-HF and below 7% in Model-RO during the most dynamic phases.

For implementation checks, we set thresholds on passing rates for a regression suite of discrete mechanics and contact benchmarks (>98% pass rate for Model-HF and >95% for Model-RO) and maintained known-solution errors within 1–2% in linear dynamics comparators.

expected_context_of_use: The context of use is to support design verification and preclinical evidence by predicting time-resolved and peak handle forces, informing whether design variants meet an internal deployment-force limit.

findings.mechanism: Unsheathing friction and stick–slip
spans: In Model-HF, the patch tests passed to within 0.3% stress imbalance for bricks and 0.5% for shells.
The Hertzian contact comparators reproduced normal load–deflection curves within 0.6% of analytical predictions over seven load levels.

The frictional sliding test recovered the expected transition from sticking to sliding at µN, with peak tangential traction errors within 0.8% for µ = 0.2 ± 0.02 and with a Stribeck regularization parameter diminished to v0 = 0.5 mm/s, demonstrating that the implementation approaches true Coulomb behavior in the regularization limit.

The linear oscillator tests gave period errors of 0.7% and amplitude decay within 1.1% over 100 cycles when using a bulk viscosity tuned to 1.5% of the critical level, in line with expectations for central-difference integration with mild damping.
findings.span: In Model-HF, the patch tests passed to within 0.3% stress imbalance for bricks and 0.5% for shells.

findings.mechanism: Unsheathing friction and stick–slip
spans: For unsheathing, halving the time step changed the peak handle force by 5.6% on average across sizes (range 4.7–6.1%); a second halving changed it by an additional 2.1% (range 1.6–2.8%).
Kinetic-to-internal energy ratios remained below 4.2% at peak oscillations, and total energy drift over the window of interest was under 0.9%.
findings.span: For unsheathing, halving the time step changed the peak handle force by 5.6% on average across sizes (range 4.7–6.1%); a second halving changed it by an additional 2.1% (range 1.6–2.8%).

findings.mechanism: Unsheathing friction and stick–slip
spans: At 40 mm curvature, the MAPE increased modestly to 10.8% (range 9.5–12.1%) with RMSE 0.34 N (range 0.27–0.41 N), driven by stronger stick–slip amplitudes.
findings.span: At 40 mm curvature, the MAPE increased modestly to 10.8% (range 9.5–12.1%) with RMSE 0.34 N (range 0.27–0.41 N), driven by stronger stick–slip amplitudes.

findings.mechanism: Unsheathing friction and stick–slip
spans: For preprocessing and postprocessing, we used a Git-based repository with branch protection, mandatory code review by at least one peer and one senior reviewer for changes exceeding 50 lines, and automated continuous integration (CI) that runs a regression suite on 112 cases spanning meshing of capsule mouth geometries, application of friction coefficients, and extraction of force traces.
Code coverage measured by line count is 82% for preprocessing and 76% for postprocessing.

At the time of assessment, there were zero high-severity open issues, three medium-severity issues (two related to rare meshing topologies and one to plotting rounding behavior), and nine low-severity issues.
findings.span: For preprocessing and postprocessing, we used a Git-based repository with branch protection, mandatory code review by at least one peer and one senior reviewer for changes exceeding 50 lines, and automated continuous integration (CI) that runs a regression suite on 112 cases spanning meshing of capsule mouth geometries, application of friction coefficients, and extraction of force traces.

findings.mechanism: Unsheathing friction and stick–slip
spans: For unsheathing, we executed a total of 18 tests for Model-HF comparisons across three device sizes (small, medium, large), two lubricity states (activated and partially dried), and a central curvature (70 mm), with three replicates per condition.
We added 6 tests at tighter curvature (40 mm) for the small and medium sizes to probe worst-case unsheathing behavior.
findings.span: For unsheathing, we executed a total of 18 tests for Model-HF comparisons across three device sizes (small, medium, large), two lubricity states (activated and partially dried), and a central curvature (70 mm), with three replicates per condition.

findings.mechanism: Frame recoil constraint during staged release
spans: The first halving of the time step changed the peak handle force by 3.2% on average (range 2.4–3.7%); the second halving changed it by 1.0% (range 0.7–1.3%).

findings.factor: Relevance of the validation activities to the COU
spans: The overall alignment reached our targets on kinematics and covered key geometric and lubricity states, but the residual differences in capsule-mouth micro-geometry and in fixture compliance during staged release likely contributed to discrepancies in peak force magnitudes, particularly for the recoil mechanism where sensitivity to local constraint is high.

spans: Ninety-six percent of 142 unit tests passed on the first run; the remaining failures involved edge conditions at high curvature parameterization and were corrected in a subsequent patch.
The contact proxy implementation was compared against an elastic ring–ring contact model; load–deflection curves matched within 1.1–1.4% over the expected range.

findings.mechanism: Unsheathing friction and stick–slip
spans: For unsheathing, halving the time step to 4.0e-7 s and then to 2.0e-7 s reduced peak handle force by 8.9% and 3.2% respectively on representative runs (ranges 7.6–10.1% and 2.6–3.9%).
Kinetic-to-internal energy ratios peaked at 6.1% during the most active stick–slip segments.
Mass scaling at 1.15 resulted in a 1.1% increase in peak force relative to an unscaled comparator; at 1.30, the increase was 2.2%, and we used this as a bound in sensitivity checks.
findings.span: For unsheathing, halving the time step to 4.0e-7 s and then to 2.0e-7 s reduced peak handle force by 8.9% and 3.2% respectively on representative runs (ranges 7.6–10.1% and 2.6–3.9%).

spans: For the reduced-order model, which relies on in-house libraries implementing connector laws and contact proxies, we managed the repository under the same Git workflow but with a smaller regression suite of 47 unit and integrated tests.
Code coverage was 58%.

Two medium-severity issues remained open during the assessment window: one concerning parameter interpolation at curvature values outside the fit library and one concerning unexpected oscillation amplification under high mass scaling; both had documented workarounds and were risk-assessed as non-critical for the test cases executed here.
